strengths: PST addresses a useful gap in multimodal NLP evaluation: gender associations may change when a text-to-image model depicts two people together. The organizational-power setting adds a meaningful dimension beyond occupation alone.

The occupational evaluation systematically covers 800 ordered prompts, balancing spatial order across 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations. The results provide substantial descriptive evidence of increased stereotype adherence under PST, particularly for male-stereotyped occupations.

Three human annotators assess each image, with strong reported agreement (Fleiss’ kappa 0.88–0.92). Providing descriptor lists, annotation instructions, and detailed results improves transparency. Checking BLIP against human judgments and avoiding its unreliable paired-image annotations is a sound methodological choice.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation exceeds what the metric establishes. SS is a signed stereotype-adherence score; opposing deviations can cancel. In Table 2, single-person occupational scores of 50 for female-stereotyped occupations and −30 for male-stereotyped occupations average to 10, despite substantial imbalances in both groups. Thus, a low aggregate SS does not establish the stated objective of equal gender probabilities within each identity. The paper should distinguish increased directional stereotype adherence from increased overall unfairness and revise claims that single-person outputs are essentially unbiased.

Sampling and uncertainty are insufficient for several detailed conclusions. The single-person baseline has only three images per identity, versus 40 appearances per occupation in PST. This makes occupation-level rankings and counts of amplified or reduced bias unstable. Organizational-power evaluation samples only 216 paired images from the proposed prompt space, and matching of role descriptors between conditions is unclear. Confidence intervals accounting for shared images and occupations, additional baseline samples, and explicit role matching are needed, especially for the smaller organizational-power difference.

The headline percentages require clarification and numerical reconciliation. Under independent, gender-balanced sampling, 75% of two-person images would contain at least one stereotype-consistent person; therefore, the reported 74.3% 'PST (Any)' rate alone does not demonstrate bias. The much higher-than-chance 'Both' rate is more informative. Moreover, under the stated binary definitions, SS equals P(Both) + P(Any) − 1. Figure 4 therefore implies occupational SS 46.2 and power SS 17.6, whereas Table 2 reports 47.38 and 18.98. These discrepancies exceed rounding and require corrected calculations or explicit denominator explanations.

Annotation agreement establishes consistency in perceived gender labeling, but does not validate whether images depict the requested occupations, power relationships, or left/right assignments. No systematic DALL-E-3 prompt-compliance audit is reported. The organizational-power template also attaches the occupation explicitly only to the first role, leaving the claimed shared-industry interpretation uncertain. These issues can confound role-conditioned bias measurement with generation failures.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the DALL-E-3 access interface, generation dates/settings, handling of any prompt rewriting, exact sampled organizational-role combinations, annotation aggregation, and treatment of 'Cannot Identify' responses. Code and data are promised after acceptance, so these omissions cannot currently be resolved through the described artifacts. The inconsistent counts of 944 versus 1,952 constructed prompts also need correction.

The mitigation conclusions are too broad for one intervention prompt. Selecting the five most biased occupations per gender creates a regression-to-the-mean concern without an independently regenerated untreated baseline. The organizational-power score of −11.12 also needs uncertainty estimates before supporting a reliable reverse-stereotype effect. These exploratory findings support further investigation, but do not establish the general inadequacy of prompt-based mitigation. The measurement, validation, and reporting concerns warrant revision before a clear Findings recommendation.
